My multi-agent harness powered by GPT-5.4 settled a FrontierMath Open Problem. The result of 2 weeks of 5-10 agents working 24/7: there are no char 3 rank 1 del Pezzo surfaces with more than 7 singularities. This is the longest coherent AI-written piece of mathematics I'm aware (230+ pages), which only makes the real bottleneck clear: Verification is key.

That's why I'm posting it here. Any help on formalizing would be great. I don't think we have birational geometry/singularity theory in mathlib yet, so any feedback here would also be welcome.

Here's the full paper.

When it comes to "correctness" of the argument, I'm pretty confident because the strategy is pretty straightforward - split up into multiple cases of geometry of del Pezzo surfaces - and as such it was great for multiple AI agents working at the same time on it. Should be much easier to also autoformalize it in pieces. Feedback welcome, and I guess this shows the glimpse into what AI in math might look like soon.
So this is nothing to do with lean per se but you're saying you want it to be? Do you have an estimate on how much it would cost to formalise the work? Have you talked to the usual suspects?

Interesting! Given that it's 230+ pages, I'm assuming that you have confidence the proof is an actually correct proof based on:

  • strategy seems plausible
  • spot-checking(?)
  • some review by independent agents(?)

I agree 100% that these types of proofs need to be accompanied by a formal artifact.

How hard would it be to get the statement in Lean? I think we have basically all the ingredients in Mathlib, or at least we are quite close.
I guess the challenging part is the klt condition?

That's exactly right, I'd love it to be about Lean, because I think verification is a clear bottleneck here. I haven't talked to the usual suspects yet, but I hope they see it here. I don't know precise cost of the formalization, also because I don't exactly know how much preliminary work we need for the gap between mathlib and birational geometry needed.

Yes, my confidence (which doesn't say there are no errors, just that they should be minor and reparable) stems from the process which was: LLMs never wrote more than 5-10 pages, and there was always a separate agent doing the verification/checking. And at the end there was a bluepring/theorem mapping and a separate orchestrator agent. This doesn't make it bulletproof, but in my experience so far it worked pretty well.

I suspect everyone's priors here are that this is probably nonsense, right? That the more informal maths an LLM writes, the more likely it is to find some plausible looking text that successfully bamboozles the verifiers, and so as length goes to infinity the likelihood of correctness drops to zero, and 230 pages is well into the "negligibly likely to be correct" domain?

I'm not trying to be rude here; if anything the opposite, that this would be a big deal / new data point about long coherent LLM generated mathematics if it were true. But your reasons for confidence in your last message sound mistaken to me.

An explanation that hinged much more on "I actually know this stuff from years of writing papers about it, and I can summarize the strategy and it sounds good" would be better. :-)

Sure, I understand your doubts, but first of all I have enough background in algebraic geometry to see I'm not getting nonsense, secondly, the verification process I've described helped me solve an open problem in the past and made progress on many others (verified in Lean).
And yes, the decay in coherence with length is a known issue with LLMs. This was solved here with multi-agent harness and dividing the task in MANY subcases that can be solved separately.

Some remarks by Opus 4.6:

...
Heavy reliance on external classification. The reduction in Theorem 9.1 leans on the Palka–Pełka series, parts of which (height 4) are only announced as forthcoming. If the external results have gaps, the foundation shifts. (The paper seems aware of this.)
...
Overall rating: 7/10 for confidence in soundness. The logical skeleton is well-organized and the strategy is correct in conception. The main risk is not a flawed strategy but the possibility of a gap in one of the many case analyses in the 150+ pages of Sections 9–12. The argument would benefit substantially from independent verification of the case exhaustions, particularly the frontier classification in Section 9 and the packet closure in Section 12.1.

@Przemek Chojecki I think the first thing you should do is to find a human mathematician that is ready to say "I think it is correct". No need to find someone that is absolutely sure, but formalization is a lot of work, even using AI, so nobody is willing to spend 6 months in formalizing 100 pages to discover there is an unfixable problem in page 101.

Anyway, my view here is: this is what we will see more of and we should have better methods to verify it automatically.

Isnt the thread just about formalizing the statement and making sure it is faithfully translated? I would not bother with the proof formalization, that can be left to the AI Agents.

I think that this is an extremely naive point of view. It is 230 pages. At the very least it will be expensive to formalize. Who is paying for this in your world view? Right now the null hypothesis is that any AI-generated proof of that length is almost certainly not 100% correct until we see substantial evidence that AI is able to generate accurate proofs of this length. Would you be prepared to pay $10K to be told "actually it doesn't work, p137 turns out to be complete nonsense"?

I am giving reading it a go, and as written some of it is pretty strangely worded and makes a huge amount of strong but uncited statements. It only has 12 references (one of which is the Epoch page), for a proof this long that seems very very little, and the existing citations are very very sparse.

Is there a way you can get it to try annotate and add a lot more citations to the statements it makes?

The first 8 sections are basically just a report on computational search and prompted by FrontierMath Open Problem and their formulation - that's why it might read strange. The real proofs start in section 9. Also there's a missing cuspidal case in Proposition 12.55 already discovered. I don't know how grave, but this is towards the end of the paper, and I believe there's enough room to make it out of there (but that's something to be revised).

Thanks for posting this, I'd love to look into it a bit more. I studied del Pezzo surfaces in my PhD, although my work was in characteristic zero and I don't know much about the positive characteristic case. Reading the problem description on the Epoch AI website makes me skeptical of this proposed solution, for the simple reason that the problem author (Paolo Cascini) seems to have expected the opposite result. From Epoch AI:

"The problem author believes that arbitrarily many singularities are possible for characteristic 3 as well".

And from the full write-up:

"A construction in characteristic 3 with more than 7 singularities would uncover a new small–characteristic phenomenon; a failure to find such an example (together with new obstructions) would be, in my opinion, very surprising as it would make the case p = 2 as uniquely wild."

When it comes to betting on the intuition of a human expert in the field vs an LLM, I am betting on the human expert every time (at least currently). But of course, the only way to settle this is through verification. For that, we would need to formalize the statement of the theorem. This needs to be done (or at least checked thoroughly) by humans, as we can't trust any AI making its own definitions. Once there is a sorry that we are sure captures the correct statement, the AI can run wild and produce millions of lines of slop, as long as it manages to prove that sorry.

The main definitions we would need are:

1) The canonical line bundle/divisor K_X of a smooth variety.
2) Ampleness of a line bundle/divisor.
3) klt singularities.
4) The Picard group of a scheme/ringed space.

None of them seem terribly hard, but all of them require a good amount of thinking about the "correct" generality to define them Mathlib-style. I think Mathlib still lacks divisors entirely, and there probably will (and should) be lots of discussion on how to make them. Of course, one could take shortcuts to define these notions in a more ad hoc way, just working over surfaces should make things a bit easier. But then we wouldn't get the benefit of advancing Mathlib, which in my opinion would be one of the main positive outcomes of such a project.
@Przemek Chojecki Could you clarify which parts of the paper are written by AI? Is it all of it, including the abstract and introduction? Or did you write some of that overview?

Interesting. I agree with your hypothesis that the proof is wrong, in case that was not clear from my comments.

My intention is that if we assume the alternative hypothesis, then the intelligence of the AI System should also suffice to write a formalized proof of the natural language proof. To be more precise I would assume that the cost of producing the formalized proof would be at most 1 OOM (base 10) above the cost of producing the natural language proof. The burden of cost is of course on the person, that makes the claim.

Assuming a 200$ monthly subscription and that he maximized the usage for 2 weeks on this problem, we get 100$. So roughly a 1000$ formalization budget, if the AI fails within those 20 weeks / 1000$, I would reject the alternative hypothesis and pronounce the proof wrong (and non-fixable). A human team of mathematicians peer reviewing the proof would be much more expensive.

A requirement for this path is of course a faithful formalization of the statement as described by @Justus Springer. In the end we just expand mathlib with more theory and move on. If the proof gets formalized, we come back. That would be my path of action.

Before even approaching the proof, I've run a lot of computational experiments to try to construct an example expected by the problem author, as he even showed what 3 methods he expects to yield the solution. None of them gave me anything and on the contrary I started accumulating arguments to prove that it's not possible.

Indeed, Proposition 12.55 + Lemma 9.41 need an additional work in the cuspidal case, or generally how cusps are treated. At this stage I welcome any birational geometry intuition. It seems I can get my LLMs to do something interesting here, but adding even more pages to the proof now, before getting experts' perspective on what really is interesting/novel/worth expanding, seems pointless.

I have not checked the whole paper carefully, so I may be missing something, but I am also doubtful. The assumption ρ(X)=1\rho(X)=1ρ(X)=1 is clearly important, since without it one can easily find counterexamples. However, at least in some places it does not seem to be used in an essential way. For example, Proposition 9.71 assumes ρ(X)=1\rho(X)=1ρ(X)=1, but I do not see where that hypothesis is used in the proof.

Hard to say, but I would be more keen to believe that there are such surfaces with an arbitrary number of singularities. Indeed, in birational geometry for surfaces in positive characteristic ppp, many strange behaviours appear exactly when p=2,3p=2,3p=2,3 (e.g. see this one https://arxiv.org/pdf/1709.09238).
I do agree that it should that the third method is the most feasible one to create an example (but it is also the most painful one to check, I think).
